title: States of Matter and the Mole

questions.chapter: States of Matter and the Mole
questions.q: One mole of any substance contains:
questions.solution:
$6.02 \times 10^{23}$ — the **Avogadro constant**.

It is a counting unit chosen so that one mole of a substance has a mass in grams numerically equal to its relative formula mass.

questions.chapter: States of Matter and the Mole
questions.solution:
$pV = nRT$, with $p$ in Pa, $V$ in m$^{3}$, $T$ in **kelvin** and $R = 8.31$ J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$.

Getting the units right before substituting is most of the work.

questions.chapter: States of Matter and the Mole
questions.q: The empirical formula of a compound of $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_{6}$ is:
questions.solution:
Dividing each subscript by 6 gives the simplest whole-number ratio: $\mathbf{\text{CH}_{2}\text{O}}$.

Glucose, fructose and ribose all share it — an empirical formula alone never identifies a compound.

questions.chapter: States of Matter and the Mole
questions.q: The concentration of a solution containing $0.5$ mol in $250$ cm$^{3}$ is:
questions.solution:
$c = \dfrac{n}{V} = \dfrac{0.5}{0.25} = \mathbf{2}$ mol dm$^{-3}$.

The volume must be in **dm$^{3}$**, so divide the cm$^{3}$ figure by 1000 before dividing.

questions.chapter: States of Matter and the Mole
questions.q: The limiting reagent in a reaction is the one that:
questions.solution:
The reagent that runs out first, so it **determines the maximum yield**.

It is found by dividing each reagent's moles by its coefficient and taking the smallest result — not simply by looking at which mass is smaller.
options: is present in the largest amount

questions.chapter: States of Matter and the Mole
questions.q: A reaction produces $18$ g of desired product from a total product mass of $90$ g. Find the atom economy, as a percentage.
questions.solution:
$\dfrac{18}{90} \times 100 = \mathbf{20}\%$.

Atom economy is fixed by the **equation**, not by how well the reaction is carried out — so a low figure can only be improved by choosing a different route, or by finding a use for the by-products.

questions.chapter: States of Matter and the Mole
questions.q: Explain the relations between mass, moles, concentration and gas volume, and calculate the volume of carbon dioxide produced at RTP when $10$ g of calcium carbonate reacts with excess hydrochloric acid.
questions.solution:
**The four relations** — every mole calculation is one of these, or a chain of them:

$n = \dfrac{m}{M}$ (mass)

$n = cV$ (solution, $V$ in dm$^{3}$)

$n = \dfrac{V}{24}$ (gas at RTP, $V$ in dm$^{3}$)

$n = \dfrac{pV}{RT}$ (any gas conditions)

**The universal method:** convert to **moles**, use the balanced equation to change species, convert back.

**The calculation.**

$\text{CaCO}_{3} + 2\text{HCl} \to \text{CaCl}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} + \text{CO}_{2}$

$M_{r}(\text{CaCO}_{3}) = 40 + 12 + 48 = 100$

$n = \dfrac{10}{100} = 0.1$ mol

The ratio is $1:1$, so $0.1$ mol of $\text{CO}_{2}$ is produced.

$V = 0.1 \times 24 = \mathbf{2.4}$ dm$^{3}$

**Why 'excess acid' matters.** It tells you the carbonate is the **limiting** reagent, so the acid need not be considered at all. Without that word, both amounts would have to be checked.

**A sanity check.** $0.1$ mol of gas is about $2.4$ litres — roughly a large bottle, from ten grams of chalk. Gases occupy enormous volumes compared with the solids that produce them, which is worth remembering when a calculation returns something implausible.

questions.chapter: States of Matter and the Mole
questions.q: Explain the difference between empirical and molecular formulae, and find both for a compound containing $52.2\%$ C, $13.0\%$ H and $34.8\%$ O by mass, with $M_{r} = 46$.
questions.solution:
**Empirical formula** — the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms.

**Molecular formula** — the actual number of each atom in one molecule. It is always a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.

**Ionic compounds have only an empirical formula**, since there are no molecules — NaCl describes a ratio, not a particle.

**The calculation. Take 100 g**, so the percentages become grams:

C: $\dfrac{52.2}{12} = 4.35$

H: $\dfrac{13.0}{1} = 13.0$

O: $\dfrac{34.8}{16} = 2.175$

**Divide by the smallest** ($2.175$):

C: $2.0$, H: $6.0$, O: $1.0$

**Empirical formula: $\mathbf{\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}}$**, of mass $24 + 6 + 16 = 46$.

$\dfrac{46}{46} = 1$, so the **molecular formula is the same**: $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}$.

**A caution.** $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}$ could be **ethanol** or **methoxymethane** — structural isomers with identical formulae and utterly different chemistry.

A molecular formula never settles the structure. Infrared and NMR spectroscopy are what distinguish them.

**On rounding:** if a ratio comes out near $1 : 1.5$, multiply everything by 2 rather than rounding to $1:2$. Rounding a genuine $1.5$ is the usual way this calculation fails.

questions.chapter: States of Matter and the Mole
questions.q: Describe a titration and calculate the concentration of a sulphuric acid solution if $25.0$ cm$^{3}$ required $20.0$ cm$^{3}$ of $0.100$ mol dm$^{-3}$ NaOH.
questions.solution:
**The procedure.**

1. **Pipette** exactly $25.0$ cm$^{3}$ of the acid into a conical flask, and add two drops of indicator.

2. **Fill a burette** with the standard alkali; record the initial reading to $0.05$ cm$^{3}$.

3. Run in alkali, swirling, until the colour just changes permanently. Record the final reading.

4. **Repeat** until two titres agree within $0.10$ cm$^{3}$, and average only those concordant results.

The first run is a rough one, done quickly to locate the end point; the accurate ones are added dropwise near it.

**The calculation.**

$n(\text{NaOH}) = cV = 0.100 \times \dfrac{20.0}{1000} = 2.00 \times 10^{-3}$ mol

$\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4} + 2\text{NaOH} \to \text{Na}_{2}\text{SO}_{4} + 2\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

**The ratio is $1 : 2$** — this is the step everything depends on:

$n(\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}) = \dfrac{2.00 \times 10^{-3}}{2} = 1.00 \times 10^{-3}$ mol

$c = \dfrac{1.00 \times 10^{-3}}{0.0250} = \mathbf{0.0400}$ mol dm$^{-3}$

**Had the acid been hydrochloric**, the ratio would be $1:1$ and the answer twice as large. The balanced equation is not a formality here; it is half the calculation.

**Accuracy.** A pipette is used for the fixed volume because it is far more accurate than a measuring cylinder, and the burette is read to half a division. The percentage uncertainty in a $20$ cm$^{3}$ titre read twice to $\pm 0.05$ cm$^{3}$ is about $0.5\%$.

questions.chapter: States of Matter and the Mole
questions.q: State the assumptions of the ideal gas model, explain when real gases deviate from it, and calculate the volume of $0.5$ mol of gas at $300$ K and $200$ kPa.
questions.solution:
**The assumptions.**

1. Molecules have **negligible volume** compared with the container.

2. There are **no intermolecular forces**.

3. Collisions are **perfectly elastic**.

4. The molecules are in constant **random motion**.

**When real gases deviate.**

• **At high pressure**, the molecules are forced close together and their **own volume** is no longer negligible, so the real volume exceeds the ideal prediction.

• **At low temperature**, the molecules move slowly enough for **intermolecular attractions** to matter, pulling them together so the real volume is less than predicted.

**Which gases deviate most.** Those with strong intermolecular forces and large molecules — ammonia and water vapour deviate badly, while helium and hydrogen behave almost ideally.

**The decisive point:** a truly ideal gas could never be liquefied, since liquefaction depends entirely on the attractions the model denies. Every real gas can be.

**The calculation.**

$V = \dfrac{nRT}{p} = \dfrac{0.5 \times 8.31 \times 300}{200\,000}$

$= \dfrac{1246.5}{200\,000} = 6.23 \times 10^{-3}$ m$^{3}$ $= \mathbf{6.23}$ dm$^{3}$

**Units are everything here:** pressure in **pascals**, volume in **cubic metres**, temperature in **kelvin**. Using kPa or dm$^{3}$ with $R = 8.31$ gives an answer wrong by a factor of a thousand.

questions.chapter: States of Matter and the Mole
questions.q: Distinguish between percentage yield and atom economy, calculate both for a reaction, and explain why atom economy matters to industry.
questions.solution:
**Percentage yield** $= \dfrac{\text{actual mass obtained}}{\text{theoretical mass}} \times 100$.

It measures how **well the reaction was carried out** — losses come from side reactions, incomplete reaction, and material left behind in transfers and purification.

**Atom economy** $= \dfrac{M_{r}\text{ of desired product}}{\text{total }M_{r}\text{ of all products}} \times 100$.

It measures how much of the starting material **ends up as something useful**, and it is fixed entirely by the **equation**.

**The crucial difference.** A reaction can have a $100\%$ yield and a terrible atom economy, if most of the mass leaves as by-products.

**Example — extracting iron:**

$\text{Fe}_{2}\text{O}_{3} + 3\text{CO} \to 2\text{Fe} + 3\text{CO}_{2}$

Desired: $2 \times 56 = 112$. Total products: $112 + 3(44) = 244$.

Atom economy $= \dfrac{112}{244} \times 100 = \mathbf{45.9\%}$ — even if every atom of ore reacted.

**Why industry cares.**

1. **Raw materials cost money**, and a low atom economy means buying a great deal that ends up as waste.

2. **Waste costs money to dispose of**, and increasingly attracts regulation.

3. **Sustainability** — feedstocks are finite.

**Addition reactions have $100\%$ atom economy** by definition, since there is only one product. Substitution and elimination never do.

That is why green chemistry favours addition and catalytic routes, and why finding a **use** for a by-product can transform a process's economics — as the cumene route to phenol does by selling its acetone.
